genes.reason: The clinically actionable CYP2C19 alleles are ordinary single-nucleotide variants in a gene with no common structural variation, so a tag-SNP array genuinely resolves them. CYP2C19*2 (rs4244285), *3 (rs4986893) and *17 (rs12248560, promoter c.-806C>T) are directly typed on consumer arrays and are the alleles that drive nearly all CPIC antidepressant recommendations. Residual risk is not CNV but 'default-to-*1' misassignment: PharmVar notes that platforms assign a default reference allele when an SNV is not interrogated, which can misclassify (their worked example is *4.002 being reported as *17), and that most PGx tests do not interrogate CYP2C19 CNVs. Rare full/partial gene deletions (*36, *37) exist but are rare. Note a genuine array-vs-WES asymmetry: *17 is a promoter variant, so it is well covered by arrays and WGS but is frequently MISSED by exome capture — for this gene an array can outperform a WES VCF.
genes.citation: Botton MR, Whirl-Carrillo M, Del Tredici AL, et al. PharmVar GeneFocus: CYP2C19. Clin Pharmacol Ther. 2021;109(2):352-366. PMID 32602114. doi:10.1002/cpt.1973. Allele/function assignments per Bousman CA, et al. CPIC Guideline... Clin Pharmacol Ther. 2023;114(1):51-68, which states CYP2C19 has 'more than 35 star alleles defined by PharmVar, including rare gene deletions'.
keyVariantsNotOnConsumerArrays: CYP2C19*37 (partial gene deletion including at least exon 1)

CYP2C:TG haplotype (rs2860840, rs11188059) — CPIC 2023 states verbatim that this haplotype 'resides in CYP2C18 (~25 kilobase (kb) upstream of CYP2C19) and is not currently interrogated by clinical genotyping platforms'
Rare decreased-function alleles such as CYP2C19*9 and other non-*2/*3/*17 star alleles, array-dependent
CYP2C19*17 is missed by typical WES capture (promoter variant) though present on arrays

genes.reason: This is the hard one, and the difficulty is structural, not allelic. CPIC 2023 states verbatim that CYP2D6 'is also prone to structural variation, including gene deletions, duplications, multiplications, and rearrangements with CYP2D7' and that 'CYP2D6*5 represents a gene deletion, whereas gene duplications and multiplications are denoted as xN'. Four failure modes defeat a tag-SNP array simultaneously: (1) COPY NUMBER — an array measures genotype at a position, not dosage, so it cannot distinguish *1/*1 from *1x2/*1 (NM vs UM) nor detect the *5 whole-gene deletion, which silently converts a true *4/*5 PM into an apparent *4/*4 or *1/*4; (2) DUPLICATION PHASING — even given a CNV count, the array cannot say WHICH allele is duplicated (*1x2/*4 vs *1/*4x2 have opposite phenotypes), because short-range genotyping cannot phase cis/trans; (3) PSEUDOGENE HOMOLOGY — CYP2D6 shares high sequence identity with the CYP2D7 pseudogene, so probes cross-hybridize and hybrid alleles are read as ordinary SNVs; (4) HYBRID/TANDEM ALLELES — CYP2D7-2D6 hybrids (*13) and CYP2D6-2D7 hybrids (*36, *61, *63, *68, *83), and tandem arrangements such as *68+*4 and *36+*10, are invisible as structural entities. PharmVar states that conventional SNP panels miss these because they target short PCR fragments and specific nucleotide positions, and that CNV assays, long-range PCR or long-read sequencing are required. Short-read WGS is materially better than an array but still not solved: purpose-built callers (Cyrius/BCyrius) reach ~97% diplotype concordance with ~96-99% call rate, with duplication-containing samples the weakest class (~90%). Short-read WES is the WORST option for CYP2D6 — *41 is defined by an intronic variant (rs28371725, c.985+39G>A) outside exome capture, and exome data supports neither CNV nor phasing.

keyVariantsNotOnConsumerArrays: CYP2D6*5 — whole-gene deletion (no-function); undetectable by genotype-only arrays and the single most consequential miss
CYP2D6*1xN / *2xN / *4xN / *17xN / *35xN — gene duplications and multiplications; up to 12+ copies on one allele have been described
Which allele carries the duplication (phase) — *1x2/*4 (UM-ish) vs *1/*4x2 cannot be distinguished
CYP2D6*13 — CYP2D7-2D6 hybrid, non-functional (CYP2D7-derived exon 1 with T-insertion)
CYP2D6*15 (and *15.003 specifically, which even dedicated short-read callers fail on due to CYP2D7 misalignment)
CYP2D6*41 — defined by intronic rs28371725; present on some arrays but absent from WES capture

genes.reason: Middle case. The core decreased-function allele CYP2B6*6 is defined by two exonic SNVs — c.516G>T (rs3745274, p.Q172H) and c.785A>G (rs2279343, p.K262R) — both commonly present on genotyping arrays and both well covered by WGS and WES. So the single allele that drives the CPIC 2023 bupropion/sertraline-adjacent recommendations is usually callable. Three things degrade confidence. First, a HAPLOTYPE-AMBIGUITY problem PharmVar calls out explicitly: 'If a particular genotype test only includes c.516G>T, an observed T variant may be defaulted to CYP2B6*6 simply because it is the most commonly found allele with this variant even though c.516G>T on its own defines the CYP2B6*9 allele' — and these two variants recur across 11 different alleles, so limited panels risk misclassifying *13, *37 and *38 as common alleles. Second, coverage gaps: *18 (c.983T>C, p.I328T, no function) is appreciably frequent in African-ancestry populations and is often absent from consumer arrays, and *22 is a promoter variant (c.-82T>C, rs34223104) that arrays may omit and WES capture will typically miss. Third, CYP2B6 has real structural variation via unequal crossover with the CYP2B7 pseudogene in intron 4 — *29 (deletion-type hybrid, reduced activity, sharing CYP2B7 exons 1-4 with CYP2B6 exons 5-9) and *30 (duplication-type) — which arrays cannot see and which even current short-read callers handle poorly. Practical note for the prototype: CYP2B6 is NOT part of the FDA-authorized 23andMe pharmacogenetics report, so a consumer 23andMe result may carry the defining SNVs in raw data while having no vendor-validated CYP2B6 call at all.

keyVariantsNotOnConsumerArrays: CYP2B6*29 — CYP2B6/CYP2B7 hybrid arising from unequal crossover in intron 4 (deletion-type), reduced function
CYP2B6*22 — promoter c.-82T>C (rs34223104), increased function; missed by WES capture and many arrays
CYP2B6*18 — c.983T>C (p.I328T), no function, appreciable frequency in African-ancestry populations; frequently absent from consumer arrays
Rare alleles *13, *37, *38 that share c.516G>T/c.785A>G and are silently collapsed into *6 or *9 by limited panels

excludedGenes.conclusion: CPIC 2023 reviewed SLC6A4 (5-HTTLPR) and issued NO clinical recommendation. Verbatim from the guideline: 'Clinical recommendations are not provided for serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressants based on HTR2A (Tables S7 and S8) and SLC6A4 (Table S9) genotypes because the evidence supporting an association is mixed and/or insufficient to support clinical validity and utility at this time (CPIC level C: no recommendation).' The abstract states the guideline describes 'the existing data for SLC6A4 and HTR2A, which do not support their clinical use in antidepressant prescribing.' Rationale (verbatim): 'While there are statistical associations and biological plausibility given the pharmacodynamic properties of antidepressants, how to translate these relationships to clinical action is currently unclear.' Contextual factors listed include unclear relationship to drug dose requirement, incomplete evidence on alternative treatments, lack of consensus on genotype-to-phenotype translation, 'inconsistent SLC6A4 L/S stratification by subvariants (e.g., LA/LG)', and differences in magnitude and direction of associations across biogeographic groups. On testing (verbatim): 'Clinical testing of SLC6A4 is available; however, most laboratories only test for the long/short 5-HTTLPR promoter variant (rs4795541), and a minority also test for the additional promoter variant rs25531. Not testing or testing for rs25531 can result in SLC6A4 phenotype discrepancies for 4-23% of long/long and 4-16% of long/short individuals, depending on race and ethnicity.' The guideline also states: 'To date, no standardized genotype to phenotype categories have been proposed for SLC6A4 or HTR2A.' Variants reviewed: 5-HTTLPR (rs4795541) and rs25531. UI note: label the panel 'CPIC level C: no recommendation' — this is 'reviewed, evidence insufficient', NOT 'not reviewed' and NOT 'shown to have no effect'.

excludedGenes.conclusion: CPIC 2023 reviewed HTR2A and issued NO clinical recommendation, under the same verbatim statement as SLC6A4: 'Clinical recommendations are not provided for serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressants based on HTR2A (Tables S7 and S8) and SLC6A4 (Table S9) genotypes because the evidence supporting an association is mixed and/or insufficient to support clinical validity and utility at this time (CPIC level C: no recommendation).' Evidence discussion (verbatim): 'Variants in HTR2A and SLC6A4 have been independently associated with response variability, remission, and side effects of many antidepressants (Tables S3 and S4). However, the evidence supporting these associations is currently mixed and insufficient to support clinical utility. Some meta-analyses revealed statistically significant antidepressant class associations (for HTR2A) or SSRI class associations (SLC6A4) with response, remission, or side effects, but individual studies often did not account for differences in medications, dose, exposure, or genetic variants that affect the pharmacokinetics of these medications.' On testing (verbatim): 'Clinical testing of HTR2A is also available; however, most laboratories only test for rs6311, rs6313, and/or rs7997012. To date, no standardized genotype to phenotype categories have been proposed for SLC6A4 or HTR2A. As such, laboratory test results for these two genes, and their implications for antidepressant response, vary across commercially available tests.' Variants reviewed: rs6311, rs6313 (promoter/synonymous, linked) and rs7997012 (intron 2). UI note: same framing as SLC6A4 — reviewed and explicitly assigned CPIC level C, not omitted.

This matters: an intermediate page-summarization step returned three plausible-looking "verbatim" quotes that do NOT appear anywhere in the CPIC paper — including "SLC6A4 and HTR2A are not recommended for clinical use" and "CYP2D6 copy number variation should be determined through appropriate genotyping". Those are fabrications and were discarded. If you re-run this pipeline, verify quotes against the source text, not against a summary. Everything in quotation marks above was grep-confirmed against the PDF.

(2) PHARMCAT AND MISSING POSITIONS — how to turn missing-position counts into a confidence score.
Core semantics, from PharmCAT's own documentation: "Any position not in the input VCF is assumed to be a 'no call'." PharmCAT deliberately refuses to infer reference. This is the single most important fact for the prototype, because it means a missing position and a reference position are NOT interchangeable, and the docs explicitly warn that running PharmCAT with positions missing vs. reference "can lead to different results."
Mechanics in the Named Allele Matcher: "If the sample data has missing positions that are required by a named allele definition, the position will be dropped from consideration." Dropping a position lowers that diplotype's score, and PharmCAT documents that missing data "is the only reason the score for a diplotype might be different between two samples." Two consequences the UI should surface distinctly:
  (a) SCORE DEGRADATION — the call may still be correct but is supported by fewer defining positions.
  (b) AMBIGUITY — when a dropped position was the discriminating one, previously distinct diplotypes tie and PharmCAT returns ALL potential diplotype matches rather than one. A multi-diplotype result is a hard uncertainty signal, not a formatting quirk.
  (c) UNCALLABLE — if every variant defining an allele is missing, that allele "could never be matched."
The VCF Preprocessor emits a report of missing PGx positions (positions PharmCAT expects that were absent from the VCF). PharmCAT offers a flag to treat absent positions as reference (0/0); the docs label this DANGEROUS and say it should be used only when you are certain the data is genuinely reference rather than "unreadable/uncallable at those positions."
RECOMMENDED SCORING RULE for the prototype: do not use a raw global missing-position count. Score per gene as missing_positions_for_that_gene / total_defining_positions_for_that_gene, and gate on two booleans that matter more than the ratio: (i) did PharmCAT return >1 diplotype, and (ii) is the missing position one that discriminates a no-function allele from *1? A single missing position that distinguishes *2 from *17 should drop confidence further than five missing positions in rarely-called alleles. Also treat "missing" from an array-derived VCF as structurally different from "missing" in a WGS VCF: array VCFs are missing positions by design (never assayed), WGS VCFs are usually missing them due to coverage/quality failure. Sources: https://pharmcat.clinpgx.org/using/VCF-Requirements/ , https://pharmcat.clinpgx.org/methods/NamedAlleleMatcher-101/ , https://pharmcat.clinpgx.org/using/VCF-Preprocessor/ . The peer-reviewed companion is Li B, Sangkuhl K, Whaley R, et al. "How to Run the Pharmacogenomics Clinical Annotation Tool (PharmCAT)." Clin Pharmacol Ther. 2023. doi:10.1002/cpt.2790 — I could NOT access its full text (paywalled, HTTP 402), so I have cited only the open documentation for the specific claims above.

(3) EXPLICIT GAP — THE "FRACTION OF FUNCTION-ALTERING ALLELES A TAG-SNP ARRAY CAPTURES" NUMBER.
You asked for this figure and I am not supplying one, because I could not confirm a defensible number from a primary source. What I found and rejected: a conference abstract (ECNP W26, ScienceDirect S0924977X24004346) reportedly stating that around half of the 149 CYP2D6 variants listed by PharmGKB are imputable from current arrays — I could not retrieve the full text, it is a non-peer-reviewed abstract, and "variants imputable" is not the same quantity as "function-altering alleles captured." Do not hardcode a percentage from it. What I CAN support: (i) Lu et al. state that 21% (44/204) of entries in the FDA Table of Pharmacogenomic Biomarkers in Drug Labelling are CYP2D6 alleles and that these "cannot be assessed fully with a genome-wide genotyping chip due to gene deletions and sequence similarity with pseudogenes"; (ii) PharmVar currently defines CYP2D6*1 through *172 (~163 distinct star alleles), CYP2C19 >35, CYP2B6 >45, against which any consumer array types a small fixed subset. If the prototype needs a coverage denominator, compute it deterministically from the PharmVar allele-definition tables against the actual array manifest rather than quoting a literature percentage — that is both more accurate and more defensible.

(4) CONSUMER-ARRAY REGULATORY CONTEXT (verify before shipping user-facing copy).
FDA granted 23andMe de novo authorization for direct-to-consumer Personal Genome Service Pharmacogenetic Reports (DEN180028, announced 31 October 2018). Search results describe the authorized panel as including CYP2C19 (*2,*3,*17), CYP2C9, CYP3A5, UGT1A1, DPYD, TPMT, SLCO1B1 and a list of CYP2D6 star alleles, with NO CYP2B6. I could NOT retrieve the FDA decision summary PDF (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cdrh_docs/pdf18/DEN180028.pdf returned 404) or the FDA press announcement (404), so treat the exact per-gene allele list as UNVERIFIED and confirm against the FDA document before rendering it. Two things are well supported and safe to state: (a) FDA's 1 November 2018 safety communication warned against PGx tests claiming to predict patient response to specific medications, singling out antidepressants — directly relevant to this prototype's disclaimer copy; (b) 23andMe's own documentation states that only a subset of raw-data markers are individually validated, that raw data "has not been validated to the extent of the data underlying our official 23andMe reports," and that raw data is "suitable only for informational use and not for medical, diagnostic, or other use." A consumer raw-data export is therefore a weaker input than the vendor's own report, which is itself weaker than a CLIA PGx assay. The prototype should never treat a 23andMe raw export as clinical-grade for any of the three genes.

(5) ARRAY vs WGS vs WES — the axis is not a single quality ladder, and the prototype should model them separately.
Arrays: fixed content, positions never assayed are absent by design; no CNV; no phasing. WGS (short-read): covers promoter, intronic and exonic positions and supports CNV inference, so it dominates arrays for CYP2C19 and CYP2B6 and is substantially better for CYP2D6 with a purpose-built caller (BCyrius ~97.1% diplotype concordance, ~98.6% call rate; deletions/fusions ~100%, duplications ~90%), but still cannot fully phase CYP2D6 tandem hybrids. WES: a trap. Exome capture omits promoter and intronic variants, which specifically breaks CYP2C19*17 (c.-806C>T, promoter), CYP2B6*22 (c.-82T>C, promoter) and CYP2D6*41 (intronic rs28371725), and gives poor CNV support. For these three genes a WES VCF can be WORSE than a good array. Recommend the lookup table key on assay type per gene, not a single global "data quality" field. Definitive resolution of CYP2D6 structural variation requires targeted CNV assays, long-range PCR, or long-read sequencing (PacBio SMRT / Oxford Nanopore) per PharmVar.

(6) SUGGESTED PER-GENE CONFIDENCE TIERS for the UI, consistent with the above: CYP2C19 array=high / WGS=high / WES=medium (promoter gap). CYP2B6 array=moderate / WGS=high / WES=moderate. CYP2D6 array=low (never render an activity score from array-only data without a CNV-unknown flag) / WGS=moderate-high with a validated SV caller and explicit no-call handling / WES=low. For CYP2D6 specifically, the prototype should carry a distinct "copy number unknown" state rather than silently defaulting to two copies — CPIC 2023 itself notes that "most research studies and clinically available tests for CYP2D6 do not determine the exact number of gene copies, which may include duplications and multiplications."
